title: Why Mendeleev Grouped Elements by Mass
topic: Why the Russian physicist Dmitri Mendeleev arranged his periodic table in groups (St. Petersburg, 1869)

lines: Mendeleev arranged elements in columns, leaving gaps for elements nobody had found.
In St. Petersburg in 1869, Mendeleev's table had empty spaces.
Not every element had been found yet.
Mendeleev left those spaces empty instead of hiding them.
Mendeleev sorted elements by atomic mass, a measure of an atom's weight.
Elements with similar chemical behavior went into the same column.
In Mendeleev's table, the same properties kept returning, column after column.
You see, it is like sorting socks by color, so a missing pair still tells you what to buy.
The real reason was Mendeleev's law: chemical properties depend on atomic mass.
Because properties repeated, Mendeleev's pattern pointed to what was missing.
Mendeleev made bold predictions about elements nobody had found.
The answer came later, with atomic numbers and quantum mechanics.
By the late 1800s, Mendeleev's table was the one everyone accepted.
Today, groups follow outer electrons, and 118 elements now fill the table Mendeleev left with gaps.

claims.claim: Mendeleev's 1869 table was the first periodic table to become generally accepted, and he formulated the periodic law as a dependence of chemical properties on atomic mass.
Not all elements were known in 1869, so Mendeleev's table had gaps, and he used the periodic law to predict properties of some missing elements.
Mendeleev made bold predictions about the chemical and physical properties of undiscovered elements.
Elements in the same group have similar chemical characteristics, and groups are columns determined by the electron configuration of the atom.
A group is a column whose elements share similar characteristics in their outermost electron shells, because most chemical properties are dominated by the outermost electron.
The periodic law was explained in the early 20th century with the discovery of atomic numbers and pioneering work in quantum mechanics.
